claims.text: A hybrid framework combining machine-learned interatomic potentials with thermodynamic integration via the Einstein crystal method will accurately predict melting temperatures and entropy of fusion for high-entropy alloys.
Sparse high-temperature ab initio data are sufficient to train the proposed machine-learned interatomic potentials.
Experimental melting data for multicomponent HEAs are sparse or unreliable.
The target HEAs contain at least five elements and initially form disordered solid solutions.
Molecular dynamics with thermodynamic integration can calculate the Gibbs free-energy difference between the solid and liquid phases of HEAs.
The intended operating regime includes temperatures approaching or exceeding 2000 K.
The intended compositional search space contains more than 100,000 variants.
An MLIP can act as a surrogate for DFT while capturing the complex many-body interactions and local structural distortions characteristic of HEAs.
Classical empirical potentials miss important many-body interactions or local structural distortions in HEAs.
Standard DFT becomes prohibitively expensive as system size increases.
Large supercells are needed to model chemical disorder in HEAs.
Melting simulations require timescales that are impractical for standard DFT.
Classical potentials are inaccurate at high temperatures because their parameterizations inadequately represent multicomponent interactions.
Learning a DFT potential-energy surface enables accurate thermodynamic-integration free-energy calculations at substantially lower computational cost than direct DFT.
Predicted melting temperatures will differ by less than 5% from available experimental values for benchmark HEAs.
The proposed method will screen more than 10,000 compositions within a timeframe feasible for high-throughput discovery.
Standard DFT would be limited to screening fewer than 10 compositions under the contemplated computational constraints.
The method is valid only when the MLIP training set contains representative local atomic environments for the target composition.
The method may fail for novel chemical combinations absent from the DFT training data.
No supplied evidence explicitly documents MLIP performance for HEA melting points or establishes the proposed thermodynamic-integration boundary conditions.
